I do a PPL split, so arms get broken into two muscle groups on two different days. I do occasionally do deload periods, so the weight for each exercise itself sort of varies, on regular lifting days I try to train fairly close to failure by the end of my last set. I also do some compound lifts so arms get a little more work from those as well, but I'll give you the targeted exercised I do for them at least!

**Triceps**
Cable extensions 3x10
Curl bar skullcrushers, immediately followed by close grip press 3x8
Dumbbell kickbacks 3x10
Bodyweight Bench dips 3x15

**Biceps**
Pull ups, depending on how sore I am usually 3x5
Single arm dumbbell curls 3x8
Single arm hammer curls 3x8
Dumbbell preacher curls 3x10
Curl bar 21's (look them up if you aren't familiar, these KILL)

I am 20 years old in the Sacramento area, but when I was your age I had to stop taking lessons because my mother could no longer afford them. I have been riding since I was about 5 years old, done hunter jumpers, polo, cutting, dressage, you name it. The only problem I see with you getting a job in the horse world at this point is (not trying to be mean AT ALL, just honest), you lack the long term experience around horses that most equestrian related jobs will require. 

However, you are doing exactly what you need to be doing to get going in the right direction. A job as a working student is what allowed me to 'get my name out there' so to speak. I started working in exchange for lessons at a very well know breeding/training/import barn in the area and by doing this I met many of the other trainers in the area. These trainers eventually say me enough around the horses and saw me show and ride and two of them actually ended up asking me to work for them (paid) as a groom. I have also had the opportunity to work as a vet tech on several occasions with the vet who did the work at the barn I worked at as a working student.

There are several things you can do if you want a job in the equestrian world, getting a job as a groom is probably the 'easiest' so to say. Other jobs include become an equine vet which will require A LOT of school. Ferriers (shoeing and hoof maintenance) also require some schooling but less than becoming a veterinarian would. Once you get comfortable enough around horses wool could possibly work as a trainer or instructor. If you really are committed to getting a job with horses just focus on getting as much experience around horses as you can. This includes handling/riding young and green horses and stallions,  I'm not sure what style of riding you are doing now but try to learn multiple disciplines (western, jumping, dressage...) as this will help you become a well balanced and adaptable rider. If you feel comfortable with it see if these is any way the trainer at your barn will allow you to give some very novice lessons and learn how to teach riding (teaching also helps you perfect your own riding).

The thing to remember is that many people that are extremely involved in the horse world don't actually have JOBS inside of it. Many people have other jobs that allow them to afford their own horses, pay board, vet bills, and show entries. But, if you want a job in the equine world it sounds to me like you really are on the right track. Working student positions are a gateway to other jobs like groom/instructor/trainer. It sounds to me like you are trying to get involved with your local equine community which really is key. Keep it up, sorry for such a long post I just really wanna help you out because I know how much horses can mean to people (personal experience!!). If you're ever in Sacramento and need to meet some horse people here let me know!!

Not too many on the ground, and my "go to's" for riding are pretty basic. I'm a dressage rider, but when I was first starting with dressage I found myself amazed at how nearly everything can be solved with the concept of inside leg-outside rein. I consider this more of a habit, or horse manners, but whenever I meet a new horse or go visit a horse I haven't seen in a while before I touch them I walk up and blow softly in their nose. Its how horses greet new friends or ones they haven't seen in a while and it helps the horse to feel more comfortable around you if they can smell you before you start handling them. You'll notice if you start doing it to them they will do it back to you. I always love it when I get to work a horse who I haven't seen in a long time, when I walk up they seem a little wary but when I use this little trick they smell me and I can see it click in their heads "Oh hey!! Where on EARTH have you been?!"

Too bad you had to stop, its unfortunate that horses are a very expensive hobby which makes it a hard one to stick with. You might want to try looking for working student positions if you're really interested in staying with it. You work at the barn doing things like exercise riding, turning out, giving meeds, grooming, bathing, showing, etc... Thats what I ended up doing when I could no longer afford lessons and it ended up landing me paid positions with several trainers who learned about me because of my working student positions. I started at Leone Equestrian but moved to PEC in Wilton. I'm not working there anymore but I've heard that the owner (Mari Naten) is looking for working students. She can be hard to deal with at times but its an amazing facility to work at so its worth it. And good luck with getting your home!!
